# How is the code laid out?

*You'll need the round's loop (chapter 1), the order book, takes and resting orders (chapter 2), the fair value
(chapter 3), take, clear and make (chapter 4), fill models and orders that arrive late (chapter 10) and the portal's
figures (chapter 12).*

## The story

The third rehearsal, the Kestrel Bourse, was built to differ from our engine on purpose. Its rules said that orders
rest, that a product may have at most three orders working, and that every lot beyond a position limit costs 0.25
credits a step. They left out what the first upload had to reveal, among it that an order reaches the exchange one
step after the call that sent it
[(`python/experiments/mock_round/round3/README.md`; `private/portal.py`, `TRUTH`)]{.src}.

Two agent sessions played it, one on the repo before its calibration tools and one after. Both worked out the hidden
rules within minutes of their first upload. Both lost money anyway: on the public sessions −4,850 and −283 credits,
on the hidden ones −3,553 and −489, where the round's own plain market maker made +325
[(`data/kestrel.csv`; `IDEAS.md`, "The kickoff prompts on a disguised round")]{.src}.

Most of the loss was not in the strategy but in the few lines between the strategy and the exchange. With orders a step late,
an order sent at one step is, at the next, neither on the book nor gone: it is on its way. Neither session's bot
counted those. So at each step it saw no order where it wanted one and sent another; the cap refused most of them; and
the room under the limit was spent twice. When the late orders arrived and filled, the bot held more than its limit
and paid for every lot over it: 2,192 credits of penalty on the first session's hidden days.

The repair changed nothing but the counting. The second session's bot with the template's `on_the_way` and `went`
switched on made +142 credits on the public sessions instead of −283 and −389 on the
hidden ones instead of −489; the breach penalty fell from 198 credits to 0 on the public days and from 25 to 0 on the
hidden ones. What it still lost was one product, BRAM, a book one tick wide where, under the round's strict matching, a
quote at the touch fills only when the price moves through it: −781 credits on the hidden days. That was a choice of
parameters, not a bug [(`data/kestrel.csv`; `IDEAS.md`, "The kickoff prompts on a disguised round")]{.src}.

That is why the bot file is split as it is, and why the split is worth a chapter.

## The idea

### The repo on one page

@fig-architecture is the whole repo as one diagram.

![The repo's architecture. A format plug-in turns any exchange's data into Days of Ticks and wraps the bot's call; the
engine and every tool work only on those. Drawn from `docs/guidebook/research/repo_map.md`, A.](../figures/f13_architecture.png){#fig-architecture
fig-alt="Boxes and arrows: the day's data goes through a format plug-in into Days of Ticks, which feed the engine; the bot file, wrapped by the plug-in, also feeds the engine; the engine feeds backtest, grid, stress, validate and calibrate; diagnose reads the Days directly; a Rust twin of the engine sits beside it."}

Two rules hold it together. The engine knows no exchange: everything that knows one lives in a format plug-in and in
the bot's ADAPTER. And every tool works on what the plug-in loads, so a new exchange costs those two pieces of code,
not a new set of tools [(`ARCHITECTURE.md`, "Architecture")]{.src}.

### The engine: one loop over ticks

A `Day` is a list of `Tick`s, each a timestamp's books, the trades printed at it and its marks
[(`python/arena/model.py`)]{.src}. `run_day(day, bot, config)` replays a day against any object with a `step` method and returns a `DayResult`: every
tick's positions, marks and PnL, every order, cancel and fill, every error and every limit breach. It is two lines
long, because it is `run_market` with one participant [(`python/arena/engine.py:223`)]{.src}. `run_market` is the loop, and
each tick goes through it in the same order:

1. If orders rest, those the new snapshot crosses fill at their own price, and each one's place in its queue is
   updated from how its level changed.
2. Each bot is called with the book it sees (the others' resting orders included, never its own), its position, the
   fills it hasn't been shown, the market trades since its last call and its open orders.
3. With a delay, the decisions join a queue and those made that many ticks earlier come out instead.
4. The bots' actions reach the exchange in a seeded random order. The cap on actions drops what is over it; cancels
   apply; the caps on new and on working orders drop theirs; then, unless the format charges a penalty instead, the
   limit check rejects every new order for a product if all its buys, or all its sells, could carry the position past
   the limit.
5. Each new order trades with the recorded book and other bots' orders, best price first. What is left meets the
   tick's market trades under the fill rule (chapter 10). In the default mode it then dies; in resting mode it stays.
6. Positions are valued at the tick's mark, any penalty is charged, and the tick is recorded.

Every assumption chapter 10 described is a field of `EngineConfig`, so a mode is a setting, not a separate engine:
`trade_matching`, `resting`, `queue` and `queue_power`, `fill_ratio`, `mark`, `limit_penalty`, `delay`, the fees,
`deplete` and three order caps [(`engine.py:118-140`)]{.src}. The default settings are Prosperity's rules, and they matched
the open-source Prosperity 3 backtester fill for fill; a test keeps them that way
[(`ARCHITECTURE.md`, "Parity with prosperity3bt is pinned")]{.src}.

### Formats are plug-ins

A format plug-in, one file in `python/arena/formats/`, is the only code that knows an exchange's files and its bot
interface. It must provide five things:

- **`PROVIDED_MODULES`**: the modules the exchange lets a bot import, such as Prosperity's `datamodel`, put in place
  before the bot file runs.
- **`resolve_data_dir`**: turns `--data` into a folder (`p3` is the Prosperity 3 data in `references/`).
- **`load_days`**: reads the folder into `Day`s, a limit for every product or an error.
- **`load_bot`**: wraps the bot file: it builds the exchange's state from a tick, calls the bot's entry point and
  converts the answer into the engine's orders and cancels.
- **`check_source`**: what `arena.validate` checks about the entry point, such as a class `Trader` with a `run` method.

Three more are optional. `RESTING`, set to true, says the exchange's orders rest until cancelled, so every tool runs as with
`--resting`. `ENGINE` holds the other engine settings the exchange's rules fix, the queue, the mark, a fee, and every
tool starts from them (`arena.cli.format_config`); a flag on the command line still overrides one. `CREDITS` is what
one unit of the quoted price is worth per lot where it isn't 1, such as the Kestrel's points at 2 credits
[(`python/arena/formats/__init__.py`; `ARCHITECTURE.md`, "Formats are plug-ins")]{.src}.

There are five plug-ins: `prosperity.py`, the stand-in the prep ran on; `drill.py`, a practice format made unlike it on
purpose; `snapshots.py` and `orderlog.py`, skeletons for shapes the Arena's data might take; and `qminers.py`, the
Arena's own, registered already as a copy of `snapshots.py` marked `TODO(day)`, to be filled in on the day by the
format swap's checklist [(`ON_THE_DAY.md`, "The format swap, step by step")]{.src}.

### The bot: PARAMS, then three sections

The template [(`python/bots/template.py`)]{.src} is one self-contained file of about 1,100 lines, standard library only,
because the competitions run one file. Its state between ticks lives in the string the exchange hands back each call
(`traderData` on Prosperity). It opens with four globals the ADAPTER owns: `STRICT` (raise on errors; the backtester
sets it), `DELAY`, `ORDERS_REST` and `MAX_RESTING`. Then the settings. `DEFAULTS` holds 71 of them, each with a comment saying what it does [(`template.py:45`)]{.src};
`PARAMS` has one entry per product with only what differs [(`template.py:165`)]{.src}. A product's settings are the two merged,
the entry winning. A product not in `PARAMS` isn't traded; a key not in `DEFAULTS` raises, which catches typos; and an
entry without `limit` raises too, because the default limit of 50 is a placeholder [(`params_for`)]{.src}. Chapter 15 goes
through the settings one group at a time.

**STRATEGY** says what the bot wants, as a `Plan` for each product: the orders that trade with the book now (`takes`)
and the quotes that wait (`quotes`), kept inside the limit as they are added. The room to buy ignores planned sells,
because both sides can fill in the same tick. `trade_product` [(`template.py:316`)]{.src} runs the same steps in the same order
for every product:

1. **The fair value**, by the product's `fair` method (chapter 3), or from an options smile.
2. **The target**, the position to work towards, 0 unless something sets it. The first that applies decides: the
   close (`flatten_from`), a fired loss stop, the volatility guard, then the target modes in a fixed order, `basket`,
   `level`, `copy`, `jump_min`, `follow`, `hedge` (chapter 8). `arena.validate` names any setting that can't matter
   because an earlier mode wins (`param_conflicts`).
3. **Leans on the fair**: the book's imbalance and the linear terms, each off by default.
4. **Take**: trade with any order priced at least `take_edge` better than the fair.
5. **Clear**: trade back towards the target with orders up to `clear_edge` worse than the fair.
6. **Make**: quote each side `make_edge` from the fair, or `make_inside` ticks inside the best remaining quote if that
   is further out, moved by `skew` against the position, never crossing the book.

Take and clear use up the levels of a copy of the book, so make sees only what is left.

**EXECUTION** turns the plan into orders, given what is already working. `execute` [(`template.py:939`)]{.src} keeps a
resting order, and its place in the queue, while a quote on its side at its price still wants at least its size, and
sends only the difference; it cancels every other resting order; it sends takes as immediate-or-cancel, so nothing
rests at a crossing price; and it keeps within `MAX_RESTING`. Where orders arrive late, `went` [(`template.py:999`)]{.src}
writes each call's cancels and new orders into the product's memory for `DELAY` calls, and `on_the_way`
[(`template.py:985`)]{.src} reads them back: those orders start the next plan as already planned, and the resting orders
whose cancels haven't landed keep their room, because they may fill first. With `DELAY` 0 nothing is kept. This is the
Kestrel repair, and it lives here because it is the same on every exchange.

**ADAPTER** [(`template.py:1010` to the end)]{.src} is, with the `datamodel` import at the top of the file
[(`template.py:28`)]{.src}, the only Prosperity code in it. It reads the exchange's state into
the template's own book, trades, fills and resting orders, and writes the plan back as the exchange's `Order` and
`Cancel`. `Trader.run`, the entry point, wraps each product in its own `try`: a product that raises is skipped for that
tick, its resting orders cancelled and each distinct error printed once, so one bug can't stop the others trading. On the day,
only the imports, `PARAMS` and this section are rewritten [(`ON_THE_DAY.md`, "The format swap, step by step", step 5)]{.src}.

### One tick, followed through

@fig-one-tick follows one real tick through those stages: Kelp on Prosperity 3's round 1, day 0, at timestamp 405,400,
with the template as committed [(`data/one_tick.csv`)]{.src}.

![One tick of Kelp through the template: what each stage reads, what it writes, and what it did at timestamp 405,400 of
Prosperity 3's round 1 day 0. Data: `data/one_tick.csv`, from the engine's run of that day and the template's own
functions.](../figures/g22_one_tick.png){#fig-one-tick
fig-alt="Six boxes left to right: fair, take, clear, make, EXECUTION, ADAPTER. On this tick the fair is 2,035; take buys 5 at 2,034; clear buys 8 at 2,035; make bids 50 at 2,034 and offers 37 at 2,036; EXECUTION sends four orders and no cancels; the two takes fill and the position goes from minus 13 to 0."}

The bot comes in short 13 lots. The book shows one bid, 20 lots at 2,033, and three asks: 5 at 2,034, 8 at 2,035 and
20 at 2,037. Kelp's fair is the sized mid, the first level each side with at least 15 lots, so the small asks are
skipped: the fair is halfway between 2,033 and 2,037, 2,035 credits.

Take buys every ask at least one credit below the fair: the 5 lots at 2,034. Clear then works the position to its
target of 0. The bot is still short 8 if the take fills, and the 8 lots at 2,035 cost no more than the fair, so it buys
them. Make quotes what is left: half a tick each side of the fair, rounded outward, gives a bid at 2,034 and an ask at
2,036, and `make_inside` leaves them there, since each is already a tick inside the remaining book. The bid is for 50
lots, because the room to buy counts the 13 already planned against a position of −13; the ask is for 37.

EXECUTION has nothing resting to keep or cancel, since on Prosperity every order dies at the end of its tick, so it
sends the four orders: the two takes as immediate-or-cancel, then the two quotes. The engine's limit check passes
(all the buys together would bring the position to exactly +50), the takes fill against the book, the quotes meet no
trade and die, and the position ends the tick flat. Kelp's PnL for the day moves from 2,352 to 2,357 credits.

Nothing in the four strategy stages knew it was on Prosperity. Under the Kestrel's rules the same lines would have run,
and the two quotes would have been on their way when the next call came.

### The tools, the twins and the notes

The tools sit on top [(`python/arena/`)]{.src}: `arena.backtest` for one run, `arena.grid` and `arena.compare` for many with
chapter 11's statistics, `arena.stress` for perturbed days, `arena.diagnose` for the data with no bot, `arena.validate`
before every upload, and `arena.sim`, a separate market that reacts. Thirty experiments to run on the day's data, calibrate among them, sit
beside them [(`python/experiments/day/`)]{.src}.

The Rust folder holds a second copy of the engine, the agent market, the heavy statistics and our bots, ported function for
function. It gives the same results to the bit, about 130 times faster for one backtest and 40 to 80 times for a grid,
behind `--engine rust` [(`rust/README.md`)]{.src}. Two copies drift unless something stops them: a table of twins
holds a hash of the Python each port was last checked against, and a stale twin is refused until the Rust benchmark's
parity run has compared every recorded field again [(`rust/twins.json`; `experiments.rust_bench --parity-only --record`)]{.src}. The uploaded bot is always
the Python file.

What the prep learnt is in three places: the ideas file, 113 tested ideas and 11 waiting, each with its command,
numbers and verdict (chapter 15); the wiki, whose 23 concept pages join the literature, other teams'
write-ups and our measurements; and the day's documents, the runbook, the on-the-day notes and the kickoff prompt
[(`IDEAS.md`; `references/wiki/`; `RUNBOOK.md`, `ON_THE_DAY.md`, `KICKOFF_PROMPT.md`)]{.src}.

::: {.callout-note title="If you know ML"}
The split is the one between a model, its serving code and a data loader. The engine is the evaluation harness, the
plug-ins are dataset loaders behind one interface, STRATEGY is the model, EXECUTION the serving logic and the ADAPTER
the input and output layer for one deployment target; `PARAMS` over `DEFAULTS` is a config file over its defaults.
Where the analogy breaks: serving code rarely changes a model's measured accuracy, while
here EXECUTION decides which orders exist at all, so it is part of the strategy's measured result. And as with
serving bugs, a replay without the delay can't show it: the Kestrel bug only appeared under the rule it depended on.
:::
